idea: Harrison's H4 marine chronometer drawn as a cutaway engraving from an 18th-century plate, with the caption 'Longitude, solved by a very good watch.' For people who like that the hardest problem of the sea was answered by a clockmaker.

A 32-point wind rose from a Portolan chart, with rhumb lines fanning out. In place of the north fleur-de-lis, a small label reads 'You are here (roughly).' Pure engraved wayfinding with one dry admission.
The Mercator projection diagram: a globe unrolled into a cylinder, with Greenland drawn the size of Africa, and the caption 'Every map lies. Pick your lie.' From an old projection plate.

Eratosthenes' measurement of the Earth: a sun, two parallel rays, a well in Syene, a stick in Alexandria and a 7.2 degree angle, captioned '240 BC. Off by about 2%. With a stick.' Drawn in code in the style of an old geometry plate.

The Great Trigonometrical Survey triangulation chain as a net of triangles across a blank page, with the caption 'Measured, not guessed.' The 1800s survey of India drawn as pure line, beautiful as lace and a monument to patience.
A Polynesian stick chart: shells as islands, curved sticks as swells, drawn in white ink on black, captioned 'The ocean, mapped by feel.' A way-finding diagram with no coordinates at all.
A mariner's astrolabe and backstaff drawn as an exploded-view instrument plate from a 16th-century navigation manual, with the label 'Pointing at the sky to find the floor.'

A map of a coastline drawn at three scales, with the length of the measured coast growing each time, labelled 'How long is the coast of Britain? Depends how closely you look.' A fractal coastline diagram drawn in code with Richardson's numbers.

An old atlas plate of the 'Terra Incognita' margin, with sea monsters, dotted coastlines that fade into nothing, and the engraved label 'Here the map runs out of facts.' For people who love the edge of knowing.

A compass card showing magnetic declination with two norths, true and magnetic, as two arrows from an old chart, captioned 'North has two opinions.' Drawn from a 17th-century magnetic variation diagram.

A to-scale diagram of Cook's first voyage track around the world, a single looping line over an empty globe with dates only, captioned '1768 to 1771. Three years, one line.' Minimal and absurdly satisfying.

The lunar distance method from an 18th-century nautical almanac plate: moon, star, ship, and the angle between them, captioned 'Finding the time by measuring the moon.' A quiet piece of clever for navigation nerds.

A pure-type design of real place names that mean something rude or funny in their original language, arranged as map labels over blank space, e.g. 'Rivière Pas Grand Chose'. Cartographic typography, no drawing needed.

A Hereford Mappa Mundi style circular map redrawn as a diagram, with Jerusalem at the centre and the caption 'Everyone's map has them in the middle.' A medieval T-O map as a gently pointed joke about perspective.
A gnomonic versus stereographic versus orthographic projection plate, three globes with grids, captioned 'Three ways to flatten an orange.' Drawn in code, geometric and beautiful.
A sounding line and lead weight drawn in cross-section on an old Admiralty plate, with depths marked in fathoms and the label 'Depth unknown. Proceeding anyway.' Bathymetry of the nervous optimist.

Mount Everest's 1850s height calculation as a triangulation sketch with baseline, theodolite and angles, captioned 'Peak XV: 29,002 feet. Nobody climbed it to check.' A diagram of knowing a height from far away.
A heliograph survey diagram of mirrors flashing sunlight between hilltops, with dotted sight lines, captioned 'Distance, measured in flashes.' Based on 19th-century geodetic survey plates.
An old chart of ocean currents and trade winds on a flat Atlantic with arrows looping around, labelled 'The sea had a plan before we did.' Drawn from a Maury-style wind and current chart.
A Fra Mauro style map redrawn with south at the top, with the caption 'Up is a decision.' A small inversion that changes how people see their own country.
